pitch_detail.notes: A tough mantle over a roof off the ground gives onto an easy slab. Stop at the point where the rock gets steeper. Linking into the next pitch is recommended. A neighbouring route starts from the same scree high point on the right and is closed and uncleaned; this route starts beside the roof on the left.
Trend up and right through a couple of easy corners and belay at the edge of a large ledge system.
Easy featured face reaches a ledge (optional belay), then a shallow low-angle corner leads to a huge ledge.
Follow a narrow rib of rock, with surprisingly good moves, to a belay on a slabby stance. Linking into the next pitch is suggested.
More low-angle rambling leads to a comfortable ledge where the wall steepens.

The Hanging Gardens of Babylon. Dirty low-angle ground gains a right-facing corner (loose rock on its left). Climb the corner, cross a slab rightward into a second corner, and belay on a comfortable ledge.
Climb the corner above. The crux comes near the top and seeps for a few days after rain; when wet, easy aid (A0) gets through it.

Easy ramp, sometimes wet after rain, then a short steep face (the crux) to a ledge; extend every bolt on that face right to the anchor. Walk the ledge to the right, make an awkward slopey mantle onto another ramp, and belay at a small stance.
Begin up the corner; a couple of crux moves reach the left-trending corner above, which ends at a surprisingly uncomfortable sloping belay. Can be linked into the next pitch.

An easy but surprisingly exposed traverse left finds a hidden bolt, then easy ground up a messy ramp leads to a comfortable ledge below where the wall steepens again. A directional permadraw here keeps rappel lines on route; clip it on the way down.
Slabs lead to a roof; big holds carry you through it to another short slab, then more technical moves reach easy low-angle ground. The belay is an acceptable stance.

The crux pitch of the route, nicknamed for Thor. The line begins on a ramp slanting left. Near its top the crux leads into a traverse rightward, ending on a narrow, comfortable ledge. A brass hammer head is glued flush to the wall here as the route's one point of tasteful aid: using it the pitch goes at 5.11a, and freeing it is about 5.11c. It cannot be removed without scarring the rock.
Step right and make a powerful mantle, then follow a long, sustained, technical face to a good belay ledge.

Easy start up a corner, a tricky stemming mantle to a stance beneath a flake, then a wild undercling and jam traverse out onto a big slab (extend all the bolts there). Work left on face holds to a ramp that returns rightward to an open-book dihedral, whose delicate stemming ends at a good ledge.

Climb a rising rightward traverse toward the big roofs. Technical moves lead to a powerful roof: extend the bolt below and the one above it and make sure the lead rope cannot jam in the crack. Sustained technical face with some jams then reaches an excellent ledge out to the left.
Step back right into the corner, follow shallow corners to a massive ledge, go beyond the rappel anchor, and belay from a second anchor placed higher on that ledge.

A steep move gains the loose dike, which you follow rightward on low fifth-class ground (extend the three bolts on the traverse). Big moves on big holds pull the roof, and technical climbing back left reaches an acceptable stance.
Ascend the slab, drifting right and going by a rappel anchor. The belay ledge is defended by a technical crux.
Start leftward to reach a rail and traverse it rightward, which is steep and tiring. A corner facing left then takes you up to a superb ledge known as the Pink Pony Club, a reasonable bivy for two.
Scramble easy loose ground to a surprisingly technical low-angle slab, then steeper, sporty face climbing to a decent stance. A directional permadraw on this pitch should be clipped when rappelling.
Angle rightward into a corner that faces left and climb it to a roof. Enjoyable moves over the roof finish at a belay on the ridge crest.
Climb the corner on the ridge crest to where the buttress angle eases.
A chossy scramble reaches an anchor where you can come off belay and walk to the summit. Take great care with the loose gravel on this ramp.

review.changed: Wrote all 23 pitches with the stated grades, bolt counts and feet converted to metres. No rappel table: descent is a single 70 m rope down the route with no station-by-station list.
review.other_findings: Stored grade 5.11a/b A0 and 23 pitches agree with the text, which puts the aid point (hammer) on pitch 12; a free ascent of that pitch is described as about 5.11c.

pitch_detail.notes: Choose a chimney rated 5.6 or 5.7, or a wide crack of 5.8 just left of it; either leads to low fifth-class ground with trees. The first two pitches can be linked, as can the third and fourth, into leads of about 180 ft.
Scramble up to the highest tree, which stands before a knobby wall split by a thin crack.
Climb the crack, then step out right over large knobs to the deep gully.
Follow the gully and belay under a good ledge below the obvious chockstone.
Tunnel between the chockstone and the wall, climb good cracks into a flaring squeeze chimney, and belay on top of the chimney. Shift the belay to the right ready for the final pitch.
A left-facing corner leads straight to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote all 6 pitches; lengths are not stated per pitch so none added. No rappel table (descent is described as rappelling the north face with slung stations, one or two ropes, with no station list).

pitch_detail.notes: The target is the pair of small roofs directly above. Starting from a big pedestal, follow an ascending crack system leftward to the first roof, get past it on the left, and almost at once arrive at a little ledge inside a shallow alcove.

Stay with the crack in the dihedral and head for the roof above, drifting slightly right. Pass this second roof on its right, then follow the crack in a shallow dihedral, minding loose flakes over your left shoulder. Easier terrain then gains a good ledge within the alcove higher up.

At the alcove there is a choice: take the offwidth overhead, or step left around the corner and work up a thin crack that gradually widens into friendlier climbing. Continue through a fine stem box in the corner system, then over easier mixed ground to a roomy ledge.
A superb hand crack goes past a block, after which the ground varies, with a web of crack systems, and funnels into a corner or wide chimney. About 20 ft of scrambling reaches a dead snag.
Get around the snag moving right onto a ledge, shuffle along it to the right beyond a block, and take a ramp into a huge alcove. The belay is below an ancient, gnarled pine.
Scramble up an easy system of ledges toward a trio of side-by-side hand cracks in a tower that faces east. The crack farthest left reaches the top of that tower.
Follow a ledge system left around a corner and scramble about 50 ft up the corner or gully to another roomy belay ledge beneath a chimney.

Climb the chimney for about 50 ft, with excellent gear in the crack on the left, until it becomes a steep hand crack in a clean wall. That crack widens to a short offwidth (a #5 is optional) and tops out on a ledge on a large pillar, facing the east summit block.
Descend leftward off the pillar into a corner, then ascend the section named The Ladder and thread The Keyhole.
Continue to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote 10 pitches; grades and lengths only where stated (P5-P10). Existing rappel table untouched.
review.other_findings: Stored pitch count is 8; the text counts 10 pitches (and mentions two pitches added to the true summit a year after the first ascent, so the numbering may differ by who counts them).

pitch_detail.notes: Only about 15 ft of 5.7 climbing, ending at a tree. The start is marked by that tree, which sits over a 5.7 crack leaning left, found at the bottom of a steep loose gully below a giant chockstone.
Traverse left across ledges to the foot of a large corner.

Scrambling ground steepens to low fifth class. Skip the tempting 3 to 4 in crack on the left (or climb it if you like) until a large flake appears on the left. Climb to the flake, which becomes a chimney; leave it with a downclimb of about 15 ft at 5.6. Carry on up ledges to a severe flake and climb it at 5.7, stemming the wall behind it. A rappel station on a horn is passed, and a good ledge above is the place for an anchor. Splitting the pitch in two helps with rope drag.
Easy going, about 5.0, through large boulders and trees. Because the rope might fall short of the top, think about breaking this into two or soloing it.

review.changed: Wrote the four pitches described. No rappel table: descent is given as alternative variants and a "may be required" extra rappel, not a single ordered station list.

pitch_detail.notes: The first lead begins below the right-hand chimney; the belayer can stand in the snow moat or on a small ledge roughly 10 ft higher. About 40 m of blocky ground with mostly good gear leads to an old piton, where a flaky face comes into view beside the short chimney wall to the left. Cross the flakes on a rising diagonal leftward for another 10 m, testing each hold gently, to a conspicuous boulder that is partly detached, with about a foot of space behind it and a reasonably firm horn at its right. Flakes sound hollow and can flex, so gear is scarce even though moves are easy. Belay hanging off the horn, wrap the boulder with roughly 20 ft of cord or rope, or make an anchor from finger-size cams in the adjacent crack. A ledge belay ahead of the diagonal traverse lets you split the lead.

Pass over the boulder and place a pair of micro cams to guard the beginning of the crux. A slopey undercling with delicate footwork swings you around the corner to the lip of the chimney on the left, and a hand-to-fist-size crack takes you past a small bulge. The terrain then eases to easy fifth and fourth class up to a good ledge below the large chockstone. Belay there, or scramble the last 15 exposed ft to the summit on the left. A rappel station sits below the chockstone.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches. No rappel table: the descent mentions one station below the chockstone and none further down.

pitch_detail.notes: Some lower-angle ice leads to a cave tucked on the left of the pillar. The belay in the cave is two pitons, which can be backed up with nuts or screws in the ice. The whole route can also be climbed as a single 60 m pitch.

Exit the cave and tackle the steep pillar; the ice ranges from fat WI4 to scary WI5+ depending on the year. Anchors at the top are uncertain, but a solid tree is there, and one 60 m rappel from it reaches the ground. If the pillar has not formed, a second-pitch alternative continues up the lower-angle gully on the right to a shorter pillar of around WI3 (uncertain). The approach and the climb both face high avalanche danger.

review.changed: Wrote two pitches. No pitch grades given in the text so none written. No rappel table (single 60 m rappel from a tree).

pitch_detail.notes: Begin on an easy crack toward a small tree below a bolted left-facing corner, then layback up to a ledge beneath a roof. Gear: three draws and singles from tips to #1.

The roof pitch. Reach a juggy fang, then a scoop gives a precarious way across to the crack beneath the roof. This boulder move can feel 12- or 12+ depending on your height. A powerful pull over the roof at a bolt is followed by an undercling back left to a small stance.
The dike mantle. Follow a thin rail to an arete and then a dike, mantle over the dike, and end with burly laybacks to a ledge. Six draws.

The power corner. Cross the slab to the right to reach an imposing corner, climb a sequency boulder problem (about V8) and a second crux transferring between cracks to the right, then a superb finger crack ends at a stance inside a corner.
Gaston through cracks to the right to reach the start of a long corner, then tricky, insecure laybacking to a tiny ledge. This could be combined with the next pitch.
The corner continues with challenging fingerlocks, the hardest climbing in the first half, ending on a large ledge below a tree.

Cracks trend up rightward and merge with the direct finish of The Passenger. Steep jugs reach a rappel anchor; from there shift left into the sole right-facing corner of the route. Belay at an anchor under the lip, or off trees past the lip.

review.changed: Wrote all 7 pitches with the stated grades and lengths. No rappel table: descent is a 70 m rope rap with one intermediate anchor, or the South Arete walk, not a station list.

pitch_detail.notes: Easy slab start on bolts, 150 ft right of the neighbouring route Hitchhiker.
Slab climbing on bolts.
Sustained slab climbing on bolts.
Sustained slab climbing on bolts.
The hardest pitch of the route, on bolts.
Easier slab with sparse bolts.
Slab climbing on bolts.
Easy ground with no protection to clip.
Slab climbing on bolts.
Bolted slab with one point of aid (A0).
Slab climbing on bolts.
Final bolted slab pitch.

review.changed: Wrote all 12 pitches with the grades and bolt counts as given. Notes are brief because the text gives only grade and bolt count per pitch.

pitch_detail.notes: The start is on a shield of rock sitting between the buttress toe and the gully on the left. Three diagonal cracks climb from right to left; midway you may swap to a distinct splitter that slants right, or keep on through smaller cracks and edges to a notable ledge. Take the centre-right of the bulge, clipping three bolts, then move right around the corner. Keep drifting up and right along foot rails, where gear is sparse yet sound, until you meet a vertical blocky crack system in cleaner rock. Climb it directly to a big ledge with trees and a bolted anchor.

Go directly up from the ledge with trees, on a blocky arete and face that take natural gear. One bolt is clipped from a big platform; a pair of absorbing moves along the left edge then reach a wide ledge with a bolted anchor.

Head up and right on diagonal cracks to the first of seven bolts, then follow the bolt line over crimps and edges that thin as you climb. Resist the urge to drift onto the easier, overgrown ground on the left, where the stone is poorer. A thin 5.11 crux ends at a bolted rappel anchor. Continue beyond it, up and leftward, into a clean crack system that crosses a corner and small roof; stubborn wedged blocks above the roof may not be stable, so take care. One more bolt precedes the anchor.
Follow the crack system for about 7 m, then trend up and right on moderate face past two bolts to a large mossy ledge.

To the summit of the feature: enjoyable face up and right past seven bolts, augmented with cams. Hollow blocks lie between bolts 2 and 4, so pull gently. An ample ledge with a bolted anchor sits at the top of the face.

rappel_detail.anchor: bolted station with chains and rap rings
rappel_detail.station: A small, good ledge reached by rappelling the fall line to the left of the climbing route (facing out).
rappel_detail.notes: First drop off the top of the feature.

rappel_detail.station: The hanging anchor you reached while climbing the third pitch.
rappel_detail.notes: The ropes hang across the hardest face moves, so rig them thoughtfully if someone is still climbing beneath you.

rappel_detail.station: The large blocky ledge at the top of the second pitch.
rappel_detail.notes: Rappel to the ledge atop pitch 2.

rappel_detail.station: The large treed ledge atop the first pitch.
Down the upper part of pitch 1, then along the fall line into a blocky, bushy corner to a bolted alcove at about 25 m.
rappel_detail.notes: Watch for the alcove as you descend.

rappel_detail.station: The alcove with bolts, followed by a massive ledge. Cross the ledge toward the foot of the climb and finish the rappel at ground level downhill of where you started.

review.changed: Wrote all 5 pitches and a six-rappel table (every station listed in order; anchors on the descent are stainless chains and rap rings per the text).

pitch_detail.notes: Loose blocky rock along the ridge top leads to a big bench.
Stay on the ridge line until a second big bench appears, facing a smooth triangular feature. A gear anchor goes at the foot of that feature.
Cross the left flank of the triangular feature, with a few exposed traverses, and end up right of the arete. A brief, easy finger crack in a corner is the last obstacle before the top.

review.changed: Wrote 3 pitches with the lengths as stated; the text says the route has many possible lines so lengths may vary. No grades per pitch.

pitch_detail.notes: Starting in the blocky saddle that separates The Temple from its west peak, climb a crack of about 5.5 and roughly 15 ft to a higher ledge holding a rappel station. Gear goes in easily.

May be treated as an extension of the first pitch, but separating them avoids rope drag and lost sight of your partner. From the second ledge, cross a questionably balanced boulder to the face, where a rusty hanger and bolt and signs of another old bolt higher up should not be trusted. A flake that once gave protection to the left of the hanger has broken away, so there is nothing to place here. A couple of careful moves left reach lichen-covered ledges, then a few moves on solid hands and feet go to the top of the face (about 15 ft); a fall here would be unpleasant. An old piton and ring at the top feel solid but are used at your own risk. Place something for directional protection for the follower. Traverse left, then climb easy fifth class for about 25 ft to the summit blocks, which protect easily in cracks on the right. The pitch can be split to cut rope drag.

review.changed: Wrote the two pitches described. The approach is 4th to 5th class scrambling from about 8,000 ft with rappel stations; not written as pitches. No rappel table: the descent counts three or four stations without a definite ordered list.
review.other_findings: Stored length 12 m looks too short for the pitches described (about 15 ft + 15 ft + 25 ft is roughly 17 m) but the scramble below is not included.

pitch_detail.notes: Start in a right-facing corner at the foot of the large flake on the north face, leading to a big platform halfway up. The slab climbing is easy yet cannot be protected, and connects a chain of ledges that rise along the flake toward the east.
More ledges, including a pleasant sequence of hand jams, reach a broad platform that serves as an excellent belay.
Take the leftmost crack up the face; it starts wide and narrows to perfect hand size, with good horizontals that take tricams. From the platform many of the neighbouring cracks are within reach.

review.changed: Wrote three pitches. Only P2 has a stated grade.

pitch_detail.notes: Climb a dihedral of about 70 ft, slinging a tree about halfway up, then exit left onto a broad base where the summit tower comes into view. Mid fifth-class rock.

Two little boulders lead up to the main tower. The exposed 15 ft section of the tower can be protected with a small cam (#0.4) or micro tricam in a 1 to 2 in horizontal crack at its base. Chains at the very top allow a top-rope to be rigged.

review.changed: Wrote two pitches. No rappel table: the descent is 3-4 single-rope rappels but the stations are described loosely.
review.other_findings: Stored length of 762 m is the whole approach and climb, not the technical climbing (two short pitches).

pitch_detail.notes: Start at the base shown in the topo photo. About 30 ft of vertical climbing reaches the vast slabby apron; then go mostly straight up, avoiding the large dirty cracks far to either side, to a decent ledge belay. Length is stated as roughly 60 m. Some loose rock and sizable runouts on this and the next pitch.

Climb the spike off the ledge and go straight up for a while, then head to the right end of the long ledge, about 60 m. Build the belay from a few cams, 0.3 to 0.75. Do not traverse left along the ledge or rocks will fall on your partner. This is the loosest pitch of the route.

The key pitch. Traverse up and left at about 45 degrees, avoiding the big ledge, to a massive crack trending up and slightly right. Follow it to near the base of the bulge, then traverse thoughtfully left under and around it; this is the crux, protected by a decent 0.3 cam. The belay is a one-person, half-hanging stance about 60 m up, just below a short chimney, a bit runout from the crux. There is a fixed nut: use it with a 0.75 and a 0.5. Another option is a belay a little way around the corner on the left, made from a nut, small cams and a #2.

Pass up the short chimney, then cross to the right and round the corner onto an easy face where the sense of exposure fades. Climbing of about 5.5 heads directly toward the arete, and a fine belay with reasonable gear waits just past the corner, around 30 m up. Only the opening 15 ft is 5.7; the rest is 5.5.
Return to the face for a run of nearly 70 m on easy, enjoyable climbing straight to the top. Belay on the flat summit behind two small boulders, about 20 ft back from the lip.

review.changed: Wrote all 5 pitches. Lengths are approximate or possibly cumulative in the text, so they are in the notes, not lengthM.

pitch_detail.notes: A bulge of about 20 m leads to the foot of a snow-ice ramp.
A long lead of about 60 m with the crux toward the top.

Hike up the creek about 100 m to the final bulge of about 20 m. Snow can be hard-angled in places and thigh-deep in others. The V-thread at the top is fairly good and can be backed up with additional protection.

review.changed: Wrote three pitches. No grades per pitch; the route grade was not copied onto any pitch.
review.other_findings: Stored length 30 m disagrees with the pitches described (about 20 m + 60 m + 20 m, plus a 100 m creek hike).

pitch_detail.notes: Climb a narrow slot with a chockstone blocking the exit. The ice here can be very thin and possibly mixed, so rock gear may be useful.
An ever-steepening pillar with a few good rests and plenty of exposure.

review.changed: Wrote two pitches. No grades or lengths for either.
review.other_findings: The text mentions an unclimbed, hearsay third pitch up the gully (rated 4+); not written.

pitch_detail.notes: First lead, about 125 ft at 5.8: follow the white-streaked, S-shaped crack past a tree and belay on a ledge just left of the crest; the 5.8 is a few face moves partway up, and the lower crack seeps and can be wet. Second lead, about 200 ft of easy fifth class: ramble up the ridge crest on blocks and through trees to a big ledge beside a boulder at the foot of the next crack. With a long rope the two can be linked.

A sustained splitter hand crack on excellent rock climbs to a tree; from there move right and continue to the next ledge. The belay is built on gear (a #1 cam fits at the stance). Some rate the crack closer to 5.8 for how long it keeps going.

pitch_detail.belay: A ledge out on the face, reached by traversing left from the horns above the paired cracks, with a small tree to anchor from.
pitch_detail.notes: The technical crux: a steep, awkward pair of parallel cracks that flare into a short dihedral. It is pumpy but there are rests, and small cams protect it well. Grades given range from 5.8 to 5.9-. After the cracks, traverse left onto the face to a ledge with a tree belay; long slings help, as rope drag builds from the traverse.

pitch_detail.belay: The station is a good ledge at the top of the pitch.
pitch_detail.notes: From the tree, find the easiest way back onto the ridge; a layback move or two is the hardest part. The more direct line starts with a hard layback and eases quickly but is sparsely protected; a short, awkward fourth-class traverse is the alternative and adds rope drag. Easy fourth class then brings you to a fine ledge below a splitter, the belay.

Start with the 5.6 splitter that rises from the ledge on the ridge crest, mostly fourth-class ground above, then cross the right side of a gendarme on an exposed traverse and continue to a ledge below twin cracks. Rope drag is the main problem on this long pitch: extend placements before the traverse, or stop short of the gendarme if the rope is dragging badly.
Stem and jam straight up a pair of parallel cracks, taking solid gear, to a good belay ledge below the final wall. A clean, enjoyable pitch that sets up the widening crack of the last lead.

A crack that widens to 4–6 inches leads to left-trending, exposed 5.8 face moves on a blank slab before reaching a jug and the ridge top. The face section is widely treated as the mental crux: protection is small and sparse, so carry wires and the smallest cams (a 0.2-size cam is valuable here) and climb it carefully.

review.changed: Kept every stored pitch label and fact; added the stated lengths for pitch 6 (110 ft) and pitch 8 (150 ft) and the separate lengths and grades of the two linked first pitches in the notes. Existing rappel table untouched.
